rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh leaders first tried to stop Muhammad’s preaching with worldly inducements, then demanded material marvels and proofs of prophethood.
rows.anchor: the leaders of the Quraysh (Ṭ, W), who implored him to desist from preaching in Makkah and sought to bribe him with worldly goods

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some understand the demand to bring God and the angels as a demand to see God directly, like the Israelites’ request.
rows.anchor: According to some, their request that the Prophet bring God and the angels is a request to see God directly (Ṭ); a similar request is made by the Israelites in 2:55.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demand for a physical book to read is also made by Makkan disbelievers and the People of the Book; the Quran elsewhere notes disingenuous demands for signs.
rows.anchor: The request that the Prophet bring a physical book that they can read is also made by the Makkan disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat that God might make the sky fall in pieces as punishment also occurs elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: That God might punish people by causing the sky to fall upon them in pieces is also mentioned in 34:9.

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The ascension refers to the immediately preceding challenge that the Prophet ascend to Heaven.
rows.anchor: Your ascension is understood to refer to their challenge to the Prophet to ascend to Heaven, which immediately precedes it (R,Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s reply means he cannot produce signs on demand and depends wholly on God for the signs he receives, like other messengers.
rows.anchor: indicates his inability to perform such signs upon demand and that he is completely dependent upon God for the “signs” he receives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly records disbelievers dismissing messengers as ordinary humans like themselves.
rows.anchor: disbelievers dismiss the messengers as“mere human beings like themselves”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers also say they expect an angel rather than a human messenger.
rows.anchor: they expect an angel rather than a human being as a messenger

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: God chooses messengers from among those to whom they are sent; because humans inhabit earth, human messengers are sent to them.
rows.anchor: He sends other human beings as messengers (R, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some say angels are imperceptible to most humans, so an angel messenger would appear in human form; Gabriel appeared to Mary as a perfect man.
rows.anchor: angels are not perceptible to most human beings (Bḍ, Ṭ), and thus sending a messenger in angelic form would not be effective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declaration that God suffices as witness between the Prophet and his opponents recurs in several Quranic passages.
rows.anchor: That God suffices as a Witness is mentioned in 4:79, 166; 13:43; 29:52; 46:8; 48:28.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 6:19 the Prophet invokes God as witness between himself and the Makkan disbelievers.
rows.anchor: In 6:19, the Prophet invokes God as Witness between you and me, meaning between himself and the disbelievers in Makkah.

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: God’s awareness and sight of His servants console the Prophet while warning the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: is meant as a consolation to the Prophet and as a threat to the disbelievers (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guidance statement and the fate of those led astray are also discussed at 18:17 and 7:178.
rows.anchor: Regarding whomsoever God guides, he is rightly guided and the subsequent mention of the fate of those whom He leads astray, see 18:17; 7:178.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read the verse as saying God alone determines human fate by guiding or leading people astray.
rows.anchor: For some this statement suggests that God alone determines the fate of human beings by either guiding them or leading them astray

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say God leads people astray as punishment for their disbelief or iniquity.
rows.anchor: whereas others indicate that God only leads certain people astray as a punishment for disbelief or iniquity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers’ rejection is portrayed as spiritual insensitivity through the image of blindness, dumbness, and deafness.
rows.anchor: The Quran indicates that the disbelievers’ rejection of revelation is the result of a kind of spiritual insensitivity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unrelenting punishment resembles the account that Hell’s burned skin is replaced so punishment continues.
rows.anchor: similar to that in 4:56, where it is said that whenever the skin of those in Hell is burned away, it is replaced with new skin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers repeatedly question resurrection by asking whether bones and dust can be given new life.
rows.anchor: the disbelievers express their skepticism about the Resurrection by posing questions about the possibility of giving new life to bones and dust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s creation of the heavens and earth answers the doubt that He can raise dead bodies anew.
rows.anchor: The greatness of God’s creative Power is invoked in response to the disbelievers’ skepticism regarding His ability to give new lives to the bones and dust of dead bodies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everything is measured by God; each creature has a term for its lifespan and judgment, and communities and the world also have appointed terms.
rows.anchor: Since everything with God is according to a measure (13:8; cf. 15:21; 25:2), all individual creatures have a decreed term

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointed term is certain, as are the Last Day, Resurrection, and Judgment.
rows.anchor: There is no doubt about this decreed term, just as there is no doubt about the Last Day, Resurrection, and Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that wrongdoers persist in disbelief echoes the description of most mankind in 17:89.
rows.anchor: For the statement that the wrongdoers refuse aught but disbelief, see commentary on 17:89

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to address the Makkans in reply to their requests for signs in the preceding verses.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is told to address the Makkans in response to their requests for signs in vv. 90–93 (R).

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: The treasuries of divine mercy may mean worldly goods that form each person’s God-given provision.
rows.anchor: refer to the worldly goods (Ṭ) that are part of the Divinely bestowed provision,or rizq, for each human being (Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, the treasuries may encompass all worldly and nonworldly blessings decreed and bestowed by God.
rows.anchor: or to all blessings, including nonworldly ones, decreed and bestowed by God (Ṭs).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Even with limitless bounty, humans irrationally withhold it because of fear of spending.
rows.anchor: even if they were to possess limitless bounty, they would still withhold it (R), irrationally, out of a fear of spending

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Fear of spending reflects an inherent fear of poverty, since creatures exist in existential poverty.
rows.anchor: The fear of spending derives from an inherent fear of poverty and need that exists in all human beings

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Human beings are miserly because their existential poverty makes them generous only with surplus, or they give only to receive something back.
rows.anchor: people can only be generous with what is superfluous to their own needs (R, Ṭs); or if they give, they give only to get something in return (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People overlook that their miserliness reflects their poverty, whereas God alone is rich and gives to obedient and disobedient alike without limit.
rows.anchor: God alone is the Rich and beyond need, while they are the poor (47:38)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Other commentators say people love good things only when those things benefit themselves.
rows.anchor: people only love good things when they benefit themselves (Aj)

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Other commentators say generosity runs against humanity’s innate disposition toward miserliness.
rows.anchor: when they are generous, they are acting contrary to their own innate disposition toward miserliness (Su).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran criticizes miserliness and urges moderate spending between prodigality and stinginess.
rows.anchor: The Quran repeatedly criticizes miserliness (3:180; 4:37; 9:76) and counsels people to spend in moderation

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators differ over which miracles constitute the nine signs; al-Rāzī cautions that the verse need not mean Moses received only nine signs.
rows.anchor: they do not all agree upon which ones are referred to here, and al-Rāzī maintains that the verse should not be understood to mean that Moses was given only nine signs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Bible lists ten plagues on Pharaoh’s people: blood, frogs, lice, flies, cattle disease, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, and death of firstborns.
rows.anchor: The Bible mentions ten plagues brought by Moses upon Pharaoh and his people: blood, frogs, lice, flies, disease of cattle, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, and death of the firstborns

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some identify the nine signs with successive Egyptian punishments, alongside other miracles Moses performed.
rows.anchor: the nine clear signs in this verse refers, similarly, to the successive punishments brought upon the Egyptians in 7:130–33

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Combined commentarial lists include Moses’ staff-serpent and white hand, speech miracle, plagues and drought, sea parting, Pharaoh’s wealth erased, water from rock, manna and quails, and Sinai’s raised mountain.
rows.anchor: the nine signs may also be said to include:

rows.speaker: a ḥadīth
rows.claim: An alternative identifies the nine signs as prohibitions against idolatry, theft, adultery, murder, sorcery, usury, slandering chaste women, fleeing a just battle, and Sabbath work; Sabbath alone is Israelite-specific.
rows.anchor: the nine clear signs given to Moses are identified in a ḥadīth as referring to the nine prohibitions given by Moses to his people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s accusation that Moses is bewitched resembles repeated accusations that Moses is a sorcerer.
rows.anchor: accusations that he is a sorcerer (10:76; 20:57

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some commentators read bewitched here as synonymous with sorcerer.
rows.anchor: Some commentators read bewitched in this context as synonymous with being a sorcerer (R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: JJ, Z
rows.claim: Others understand Pharaoh to accuse Moses of being misled or confused by sorcery.
rows.anchor: others suggest that here Pharaoh is accusing Moses of being misled or confused by sorcery (JJ, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baṣāʾir literally means insights or perceptions and can describe signs that should make people perceive the truth.
rows.anchor: Clear portents here renders baṣāʾir

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: Other commentators gloss the portents as clear arguments or proofs for Moses’ prophethood.
rows.anchor: clear arguments or proofs for the truthfulness of Moses’ prophethood (IK, R)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another gloss is clear indications of God’s power and oneness.
rows.anchor: clear indications of God’s Power and Oneness (Q).

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Pharaoh knew the signs came from God; anyone reasoning properly would see their divine origin, and only willful stubbornness prevented acceptance.
rows.anchor: it should be obvious to any who use their intellect that such signs could only be Divine in origin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathbūr, rendered doomed, can also mean destroyed, deprived of all good, or lacking reason or intelligence.
rows.anchor: Doomed translates mathbūr, which can also mean “destroyed” (cf. 25:13–14; R, Ṭ), prevented from all goodness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s attempt to expel Moses and the Israelites parallels Quraysh’s attempt against Muhammad.
rows.anchor: That Pharaoh desired to incite Moses and the Israelites from the land parallels the desire of the Quraysh to incite the Prophet Muhammad from Makkah

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: To incite them from the land can mean removing them by exile or killing them.
rows.anchor: removing them from the land by either exiling or killing them (Q, R)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase can mean harassing them until they leave.
rows.anchor: inciting them to leave as a result of harassment (Ṭs).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yastafizza is also used of Satan’s attempt to incite people and may mean unsettle or disturb.
rows.anchor: mean to “unsettle” or “disturb.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s drowning warns Quraysh of the fate awaiting rejection and persecution.
rows.anchor: served as a warning to the Quraysh of the fate that might await them if they continued to reject Muhammad and persecute his followers

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Although Pharaoh sought to eliminate Moses and Israel, he and his supporters drowned, illustrating that evil plotting harms its authors.
rows.anchor: evil plotting besets none but its authors (35:43; R).

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The command to settle the land may mean settling parts of Egypt after Pharaoh’s removal.
rows.anchor: their settling parts of the land of Egypt, now devoid of Pharaoh and his supporters (Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Another view identifies the land as Palestine, or Canaan.
rows.anchor: their settling in Palestine (Canaan; Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A further view allows that the Israelites settled both Egypt and Palestine.
rows.anchor: or to both (Q); see 7:137c.

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: In context, Israel’s settling may promise the Prophet Islam’s future conquest of Makkah.
rows.anchor: this verse can be understood as a glad tiding to the Prophet of the future conquest of Makkah for Islam (IK).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: A mixed assembly may mean diverse Israelites, both noble and base, obedient and disobedient, pious and sinful, strong and weak.
rows.anchor: meaning that there will be various types of people among them—noble and base, obedient and disobedient, pious and iniquitous, strong and weak (R)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Alternatively, God will bring the Israelites and their enemies together for judgment.
rows.anchor: or that God will bring them and their enemies together for judgment on that day (IK).

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Sending the Quran in truth means it commands justice and virtue and forbids injustice and wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: justice and virtue and forbidding injustice and iniquity(Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The phrase also means no one can alter the Quran.
rows.anchor: the impossibility of anyone altering it (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran calls Muhammad a bearer of glad tidings and warner, as it does all earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: The Quran attests in many verses that the Prophet has been sent as a bearer of glad tidings and as a warner

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Dividing the Quran into parts refers to gradual revelation to Muhammad, allowing him to recite it at intervals.
rows.anchor: the successive and gradual revelation of the Quranic verses to the Prophet (JJ,Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some say the entire Quran descended to the lower heaven on Laylat al-Qadr, then was revealed to Muhammad over twenty-three years.
rows.anchor: the Quran was sent down as a whole to the lower heavens in a single night (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some understand the whole Quran to have entered the Prophet’s heart on that night and then been gradually revealed to his consciousness.
rows.anchor: The Quran is also understood by some as having been sent down as a whole into the very heart of the Prophet

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: The Quran’s division can also mean its organization into verses or surahs of unequal length.
rows.anchor: the division of the Quran into distinct sections (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Discrete revelation gave people time to learn, memorize, and understand the Quran properly.
rows.anchor: so that they would have time to learn it properly, memorize it, and come to understand it (Bḍ, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gradual revelation also made Muhammad’s heart firm, and the text affirms that gradual descent was divinely intended.
rows.anchor: It is so, that We may make firm thine heart thereby. And We have recited it unto thee in a measured pace

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Ṭ
rows.claim: The command to believe or not means the Makkans’ response has no effect on God and their rejection cannot harm Him.
rows.anchor: their belief or disbelief has no effect upon God (Bḍ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Those given prior knowledge means the People of the Book, or some of them, who recognize the Quran’s divine origin and are nobler than pagan Makkans.
rows.anchor: those who were given knowledge before, meaning the People of the Book, or at least some of them, are said to recognize the Quran’s Divine provenance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book recognize the Quran as they recognize their own children.
rows.anchor: the People of the Book are said to recognize the Quran as they recognize their own children

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: For pious People of the Book, Quran recitation softens their hearts and moistens their faces, as in the description of Christians.
rows.anchor: the recitation of the Quran “softens their hearts and moistens their faces”(Z)

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: They prostrate in gratitude for living to see the Prophet described in their scriptures.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn Kathīr, when it is recited unto them they fall down prostrate in gratitude for having lived to see the Prophet as described in their scriptures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humility and obedience on hearing the Quran mark believers; failure to prostrate indicates disbelief.
rows.anchor: Demonstrating humility and obedience upon hearing the Quran is the response of believers, and thus the failure to do so is indicative of disbelief

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The People of the Book’s praise may acknowledge God’s promise to send a future prophet.
rows.anchor: may refer to the fulfillment of His Promise to send a future prophet to guide them (Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere God’s promise is fulfilled at the apocalypse, and the Quran repeatedly asserts that His promise is true.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere, God’s Promise is said to be fulfilled at the time of the apocalypse (73:18), and the Quran repeatedly asserts that the Promise of God is true

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Some explain the People of the Book’s weeping prostration as humility before God and belief in His Book and Prophet.
rows.anchor: because of their humility toward God and their belief in His Book and His Prophet (IK)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Another explanation is that they are deeply moved by the Quran’s teachings.
rows.anchor: the teachings of the Quran(Bḍ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets and descendants of Noah and Abraham also prostrate and weep when encountering the Compassionate’s signs.
rows.anchor: describes the prophets and progeny in the line of Noah and Abraham as falling down prostrate and weeping upon encountering the signs of the Compassionate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People’s responses to Quran recitation and divine signs reveal their inward belief or hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: the different responses of individuals to hearing the Quran or to encountering the signs of God in any form are indicative of their inward state of belief or hypocrisy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God and al-Raḥmān are both divine names; al-Raḥmān is a name of the Essence and also functions as a proper name.
rows.anchor: the latter, one of the most important Names of God, is considered a Name pertaining to the Divine Essence

rows.speaker: Bḍ, IK
rows.claim: One report says the verse followed idolaters hearing the Prophet call on Allah and al-Raḥmān, then accuse him of invoking two gods.
rows.anchor: invoking two separate Divine beings (Bḍ, IK)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, IK
rows.claim: Another account has the Prophet call al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm, prompting the same accusation; the verse clarifies the names refer to one God.
rows.anchor: invoking two separate Divine beings (Bḍ, IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Most Beautiful Names are mentioned elsewhere, and their significance spans Muslim belief, practice, and piety.
rows.anchor: The mention of God’s Most Beautiful Names is also found in 7:180; 20:8; 59:24.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer should avoid loudness and show reverence and humility; some connect this with commands not to raise voices before the Prophet during prayer.
rows.anchor: One should be not loud in . . . prayer (see also 7:205), but rather demonstrate reverence and humility when praying

rows.speaker: Bḍ, IK
rows.claim: Some say quiet recitation protects the sacred prayer from idolaters overhearing and cursing or disparaging it.
rows.anchor: the idolaters overhear the prayer and respond by cursing or disparaging the sacred act (Bḍ, IK).

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Prayer should not be too quiet, so that beneficiaries can hear; an imam must be audible to those behind him.
rows.anchor: the imām, or prayer leader, should not recite so quietly that it is inaudible to those praying behind him (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: One report applies the instruction to personal supplication, although ṣalāh usually means canonical prayer.
rows.anchor: this injunction pertains to personal supplicatory prayer (duʿāʾ), although the verse uses ṣalāh, which usually designates the canonical prayer (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The middle way in prayer reflects Quranic moderation, the middle community, and the straight path.
rows.anchor: One should seek a way between is consistent with the Quran’s exhortation toward moderation in other matters

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: He says one should avoid loud prayer as ostentation and quiet prayer out of fear of others.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn ʿAbbās, one should not pray loudly, so as to make an ostentatious display for other people, or too quietly, out of fear of them (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran denies that God has a child, refuting Christian claims about Jesus, Jewish and Christian claims of being God’s children, and pagan claims of divine daughters.
rows.anchor: That God has no child is a frequent assertion of the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has no protector out of lowliness because He needs no one’s aid or support.
rows.anchor: means that God neither seeks nor needs the aid or support of anyone, as a lowly person might for his own protection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proclaiming God’s greatness can mean reciting Allāhu akbar, the takbīr, in prayer and other rituals.
rows.anchor: The takbīr is recited ritually at the initiation of each canonical prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The takbīr also expresses joy at religious milestones and summons strength and unity in challenges, battle, and victory.
rows.anchor: as an exclamation of joy at religiously significant events

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Some describe the Quran as God’s greatest gift to humanity because it brings people from darkness into light; the servant is the Prophet.
rows.anchor: described by some as God’s greatest gift to humanity, since it brings them from darkness into light (IK). His servant refers to the Prophet.

rows.speaker: Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: The Quran’s lack of crookedness means it has no contradictions or discrepancies.
rows.anchor: widely understood to mean that it contains no contradictions or discrepancies (Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Others understand the phrase as denying corruption or falsehood in the Quran.
rows.anchor: understood to mean that the Quran contains no corruption or falsehood (R, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The Quran also remains continuously beneficial and guides people toward the straight path.
rows.anchor: that it remains continuously beneficial (Ṭs) as it guides people toward the straight path (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qayyim describes religion elsewhere but here describes the Book as upright, straight, harmonious, balanced, and incorruptible.
rows.anchor: Upright translates qayyim, which is used elsewhere

rows.speaker: Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Some read qayyim as the Quran’s custodianship of earlier scriptures: confirming their truth, removing falsehood, and abrogating some laws.
rows.anchor: some thus interpret it to mean that the Quran is a custodian of earlier scriptures, a confirmer of them, and a witness to their truth

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Others understand the Quran as custodian of people’s welfare and religious affairs.
rows.anchor: The Quran can also be understood as a “custodian” of people’s welfare (R, Z) and of religious affairs

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: The Quran is qayyim because it is perfect in itself and perfects something else.
rows.anchor: the Quran is described as qayyim, because it is both perfect in itself and something that perfects something else

rows.speaker: al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār
rows.claim: He argues these verses support the Muʿtazilite view that the Quran is created: descent and being made upright imply change and making, unlike the eternal uncreated Quran of the Ashʿarites.
rows.anchor: the Muʿtazilite theologian al-QāḍīʿAbd al-Jabbār argued

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran warns and gives glad tidings, the paired missions of prophets and messengers.
rows.anchor: This Book was sent down as a means by which the Prophet could both warn and give glad tidings—the twin vocations of all messengers and prophets

rows.speaker: Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: The beautiful reward is the Garden of Paradise.
rows.anchor: The beautiful reward refers to the paradisal Garden (Ṭs, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking a child is an idiom for assuming paternal responsibility or taking someone into one’s care, criticizing even the idea of a special adoptive relationship with God.
rows.anchor: a Quranic idiom meaning to assume special paternal responsibility for a child, to recognize a child, to take the child to oneself or into one’s care

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran rejects divine offspring claims, likely the Makkan belief that angels are God’s daughters, while also addressing Jewish and Christian claims.
rows.anchor: Given that this is a Makkan sūrah, however, these verses are likely referring to the idolatrous belief regarding the angels (IK).

rows.speaker: Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Those making this claim lack knowledge; they blindly imitate their ancestors instead of thinking independently.
rows.anchor: their claim derives not from knowledge, but from gross ignorance and blindly following the belief of their ancestors without exercising independent thought

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Calling the claim monstrous expresses its moral gravity.
rows.anchor: expresses the moral gravity of this claim (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Calling it monstrous also conveys the shock such a claim should elicit.
rows.anchor: as well as the shock and surprise that such a claim should elicit (Z).

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Saying the claim issues from their mouths stresses that it is fabricated and has no valid source.
rows.anchor: emphasizes that it is something completely fabricated for which they have no valid source (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A near-identical statement appears at 26:3.
rows.anchor: Cf. 26:3, which contains a nearly identical statement.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Destroying oneself with grief can mean expending or utterly exhausting oneself in concern and sadness for disbelievers.
rows.anchor: To destroy thyself with grief could also mean “to expend thyself in grief” (R), that is, to utterly exhaust oneself with concern and sadness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet grieves over the Makkans’ rejection and repeated requests for signs; other passages console him that their rejection is of God’s signs.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is frequently presented in the Quran as being distraught by the failure of the Makkans to accept the message he had brought them

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Earth’s adornment includes its plants, animals, gold, and metals; al-Rāzī considers humanity its noblest creature.
rows.anchor: The earth is “adorned” by the various phenomena found upon it or in it, including its flora and fauna and its precious gold and metals

rows.speaker: Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazzālī
rows.claim: Earthly adornment tests whether people maintain detachment and asceticism toward the world.
rows.anchor: the “adornment” of the earth is a means by which God tries human beings with regard to their ability to maintain an attitude of detachment and asceticism toward the world

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The barren plain means earthly adornments will not last but will end and return to God.
rows.anchor: none of its adornments will endure forever, but will come to end and return to God (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave story answered a Quraysh challenge; reportedly unfamiliar with it, the Prophet waited a long time for revelation to answer the skeptics.
rows.anchor: This account was revealed to the Prophet in response to a challenge issued by the Quraysh. The Prophet was reportedly unfamiliar with this story

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account resembles the Christian Seven Sleepers of Ephesus story in its details and in presenting resurrection as proof of God’s power.
rows.anchor: also known in Christian tradition as the “Seven Sleepers of Ephesus.” The Quranic and Christian accounts are very similar

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Following the consolation in verse 6, the story may suggest that God will deliver Muhammad and his followers as He saved persecuted believers.
rows.anchor: just as God saved this small group of believers during a time of persecution, so too would He deliver the Prophet and his followers (Ṭs).

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The youths fled worldly goods to preserve faith, a voluntary death to the world that follows the earth’s adornments as a trial.
rows.anchor: the youths of the cave who fled all earthly goods and benefits to preserve their faith (Ṭs), suggesting a kind of voluntary death to the world

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Because the youths were pious nonprophets protected through miraculous sleep, the story supports the possibility of saintly karāmāt distinct from prophetic miracles.
rows.anchor: the story is adduced by some as

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The rhetorical question implies that greater signs include creation of the heavens and earth; if the story is a karāmah, ordinary nature may be an even greater wonder.
rows.anchor: there are other “signs” that are even more wondrous in nature, such as God’s creation of the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Al-kahf can mean a particularly spacious cave in a mountain.
rows.anchor: al-kahf, which is said to designate more specifically a very spacious cave situated in a mountain (R, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Many commentators identify al-raqīm as a lead tablet at the cave entrance or an inscription carved nearby recounting the youths’ story.
rows.anchor: al-raqīm here refers to an inscription made on a leaden tablet placed at the entrance of the cave or an inscription carved into the mountain

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another proposal is that al-raqīm names a book containing Christian laws and teachings.
rows.anchor: al-raqīm in this passage refers to a book containing the laws and teachings of Christianity (Q)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Other commentators identify al-raqīm as the valley, mountain, or region where the cave lay; proposed locations include northwest Arabia and southern Palestine, Ephesus, or Jordan.
rows.anchor: al-raqīm refers to the name of the valley, the mountain, or the region in which the cave was located

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: One view identifies al-raqīm as the building erected to commemorate the cave.
rows.anchor: commemorate the cave (IK), the name of

rows.speaker: ST
rows.claim: Another view says al-raqīm is the name of the companions’ leader.
rows.anchor: the name of the leader of the companions (ST)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: A further view identifies al-raqīm as the companions’ dog.
rows.anchor: the name of their dog (Z; see 18:18c)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: A clear authority is proof that the alleged deities merit worship; the verse supports grounding worship in reason rather than blind imitation.
rows.anchor: for some this verse supports the important Islamic principle that religious worship must be based upon intellectual proof and should not derive solely from blind imitation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fabricating a lie against God here means associating partners with Him, a charge repeated elsewhere.
rows.anchor: in this case, by ascribing partners to Him, is repeated in several verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse discourages debate over the youths’ number because it is speculation about the unseen, which belongs to God.
rows.anchor: all such debate amounts to guessing at the unseen, a vain endeavor

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Some identify the few who know the youths’ number as the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: Some identify the “few” here as the People of the Book (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The command to dispute only with clear argument addresses the Prophet, who should let the Quranic account suffice instead of debating them.
rows.anchor: instructs him not to debate with them about the matter, but rather to let the parts of the story that had been revealed to him in this Quranic account suffice

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The Prophet is also told not to question the People of the Book further about the story.
rows.anchor: meaning that he should not question the People of the Book further about this matter (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith and righteous deeds are repeatedly paired as bases for success in this world as it bears on the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Believing and performing righteous deeds are frequently mentioned together as the twin bases of success in this world as far as it affects life in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran likewise promises not to waste the reward of believers and righteous workers.
rows.anchor: the same is said for the believers (3:171) and the workers of righteousness (7:170).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Gabriel hadith presents belief, submission through the five pillars, and virtue as the religion’s three components: īmān, islām, and iḥsān.
rows.anchor: Belief, submission through the performance of righteous deeds, and virtue represent the three basic components of religion—īmān, islām, and iḥsān—according to the well-known ḥadīth of Gabriel
